content.rationale:
`src/draft_identity.rs` is the one implementation of the content identity the record's base carries. Its commitment is exact: `identity(bytes)` is the SHA-256 of exactly the bytes it is given, rendered as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters with no prefix, separator or decoration; `base(contents)` takes an owned set's repo-relative paths together with their content and returns exactly one entry per path supplied, each the identity of that path's content and nothing else — no path name, node id, change id or other metadata folded into the value, and no framing, re-encoding, newline normalisation or trimming of the bytes before they are hashed.

S5-identity (skooqvul) fixes the value space this module renders: the FIPS 180-4 SHA-256 of the path's content byte for byte, 32 output bytes written high nibble first as two lowercase hex digits each, one-way, equal content giving an equal identity, with nothing of the path, the change or the workspace in the input and the bytes not framed, re-encoded, newline-normalised or trimmed. The module adds no rule to that value space: `identity` hands the caller's slice to the digest untouched, so a trailing newline, a trailing space and a CRLF pair are hashed rather than tidied, because trimming or newline folding would hash content the path does not hold and the identity would describe bytes that were never read. S5-base (qrqsxyzz) fixes that a base is a value per path of the owned set, determined by that path's content and by nothing else, one entry for every path the set holds; `base` therefore keys the map by the repo-relative path and hashes only that path's bytes, so two paths carrying the same content carry the same identity value, the value is content-addressed rather than path-addressed, and an empty owned set yields an empty base. S4-base (zsvukpls) states that requirement at the opening — one entry for every path the set holds, each the identity of that path's content — and this module is the implementation that requirement names; when the base is taken, and that it is taken at the opening, stay with that node.

zutqsqtu's journal supplies the digest. `crate::journal::sha256_hex` is the journal store's FIPS 180-4 SHA-256 and its lowercase hex rendering, and this module reuses it through `use crate::journal::sha256_hex;` rather than carrying a second digest in the crate, so the base and the journal's content-addressed blobs are one function and there is nothing here to drift from it: a change to the digest reaches both, and a reader has one implementation to trust rather than two. The alternative — carrying a second SHA-256 in `src/draft_identity.rs` — would compile and answer the same published vectors today, and that is exactly what it risks: two statements of one rule that can part later, after which the base and the journal disagree about what the same bytes hash to and neither is obviously wrong. The digest is therefore imported rather than restated, and the module contributes only the projection from bytes, and from paths with bytes, to identities; the one algorithm stays where zutqsqtu put it.

lwnnssuo fixes what the owned set is — the node document plus the repo-relative paths the node's `content.ref` lists when `ref` is an array, attributed through the ownership rule and never by scanning — and osplmlvq fixes the read that produces each path's content, a file's bytes at a named revision. This module sits below both: `base` receives the already-resolved paths and their bytes and makes no jj call, reads no working copy and derives no ref list, so the set, the change it is read at and who owns each path are decided above it and cannot be re-derived or guessed here. szmuyqrq (M-layout) places the module flat at `src/draft_identity.rs`, one file with the module tree declared at the crate root, and knqkxzns (M-tests) is why that shape matters: a self-contained test crate pulls modules in by the paths they sit at, so `crate::journal` names the journal the binary compiles and the reuse resolves in the binary's tree and in a test tree alike, while a std-only leaf would still compile if the module had been written that way.

Deliberately not here. The module writes no record and encodes no base: the record model, its JSON and the field that holds the base belong to the record nodes above it, and the module returns an ordinary `BTreeMap` keyed by path so the entries are ordered by path wherever that layer renders them. It does not compare a base with a later owned set, name differing paths or decide what a stale draft may do, which are the landing rules of qrqsxyzz. It does not choose the moment the base is taken, and it does not read content from jj; it maps bytes to identities and paths with bytes to a base, and that is the whole of what the layer depends on it for.
